James Watt, born in 1736 and died in 1819, was a Scottish engineer and inventor whose improvements to the steam engine proved transformative for the Industrial Revolution. Though he did not invent the steam engine itself, his design innovations—particularly the separate condenser—vastly improved efficiency and practical utility, making steam power economically viable for manufacturing and transportation. Watt represents the intersection of Scottish Enlightenment intellectual culture and entrepreneurial energy that propelled Britain's industrial dominance.

Watt was born in Greenock, Scotland, and trained as an instrument maker, acquiring practical knowledge that shaped his engineering approach. In 1765, while repairing a Newcomen steam engine, he conceived of the separate condenser, which eliminated the energy waste of heating and cooling the cylinder repeatedly. He partnered with Matthew Boulton of Birmingham, forming the Boulton and Watt company in 1775, which became the era's leading steam engine manufacturer. Their innovations standardized horsepower as a unit of measurement.

His improvements reduced fuel consumption by up to seventy-five percent compared to earlier designs, making steam power practical for textile mills, metalworks, and other industries. Watt was a prolific inventor beyond the steam engine, holding patents for rotative motion, parallel motion mechanisms, and other mechanical innovations. He was part of the Lunar Society of Birmingham, a club of Enlightenment intellectuals and industrialists that included Erasmus Darwin, Josiah Wedgwood, and Matthew Boulton, representing the fusion of science and manufacturing.

The separate condenser allowed the cylinder to remain at operating temperature continuously, unlike Newcomen engines which repeatedly lost heat, wasting fuel and reducing efficiency dramatically. Boulton and Watt became enormously profitable, holding monopolies on steam engine patents for decades and extracting royalties based on fuel savings, creating an unprecedented business model. Watt's improvements made steam engines practical for textile mills, metalworks, breweries, and eventually railways, directly enabling the Industrial Revolution's factory system. Though Scottish, Watt's greatest influence came through his partnership with Boulton in Birmingham, which became the hub of British manufacturing innovation.
